meta.blurb: Grace, sixty-three, trips on a kerb. She is not hurt, but she is frightened. Her neighbour Mateo, a physiotherapist, teaches her ten everyday moves, from walking to getting up off the floor, and how to practise each one safely.
meta.bible: Grace: a sixty-three-year-old retired teacher who trips on a kerb and decides to look after her body, the main character. Mateo: her neighbour, a Physiotherapist in his forties, kind, calm and practical. Setting: a quiet street of terraced houses, Grace's small garden, a local park with a bench, and her living room. The ten moves: Walk, Sit to stand, Hinge, Push, Pull, Carry, Climb, Twist, Balance and Floor. Key terms: Kerb, Physiotherapist, Brisk, Posture, Grip, Falls, Tai chi, Flexibility, Stairs, Counter, Hips, Shoulders, Spine, Stretch, Warm-up. Voice: warm, simple and encouraging, one idea in each beat, with the ten moves explained in four beats each. The advice is general and hedged: people differ, some conditions need a doctor's advice, and none of it is a diagnosis or a personal plan. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

beats.scene: Grace catches her foot on a kerb and steadies herself on a lamp post
beats.summary: Grace, sixty-three, trips on a kerb and is not hurt, but she is frightened and wants to stay strong for life.

beats.scene: Mateo, a neighbour in a blue jacket, talks to Grace over a garden fence
beats.summary: Her neighbour Mateo, a physiotherapist, says that the body is built to move and that ten basic moves cover most of daily life.

beats.scene: A woman sits on a sofa while the clock moves on
beats.summary: Modern life involves a great deal of sitting, and long unbroken sitting is linked with poorer health.

beats.scene: A chart showing a week with a few short walks marked along it
beats.summary: Health guidelines suggest 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, and some movement is better than none.

beats.scene: Grace walks along a tree-lined street with a friendly nod to a neighbour
beats.summary: Move one is walking, which is the base of all movement and needs no equipment.

beats.scene: Two people in running shoes walk fast and talk side by side
beats.summary: A brisk walk is one where you can talk but could not sing, and it counts as moderate activity.

beats.scene: A heart drawn on a notepad beside a pair of walking shoes
beats.summary: Regular walking is linked with a healthier heart and better mood, and with living longer.

beats.scene: Grace sets a kitchen timer and ties her shoes at the door
beats.summary: Start with ten minutes a day and add a little each week.

beats.scene: Grace starts to stand from a firm kitchen chair, arms forward
beats.summary: Move two is sit to stand, which is the squat of daily life: getting up from a chair or a toilet.

beats.scene: Mateo stands beside Grace as she rises from a chair with her feet apart
beats.summary: To do it, put your feet under your knees, lean forward a little and stand by pushing through your feet.

beats.scene: A stopwatch beside a chair with a smiling Grace counting aloud
beats.summary: A common test is how many times you can stand up in thirty seconds, but it is a rough guide only.

beats.scene: Grace stands up from a chair ten times while her neighbour watches the clock
beats.summary: Practise a few stands each day, then make it harder with slower lowering or by holding a weight.

beats.scene: Grace bends at the hips to pick up a basket, back straight
beats.summary: Move three is the hinge: bending at the hips to pick things up from the floor without stressing the back.

beats.scene: Mateo shows Grace how to push her hips back, hands on thighs
beats.summary: To hinge, push your hips back, keep your back long, and let your knees bend a little.

beats.scene: Grace lifts a bag of compost in her garden with bent knees
beats.summary: Use the hinge when lifting objects: keep the load close to your body and stand up using your legs and hips.

beats.scene: Grace touches a low shelf in her kitchen after a controlled hinge
beats.summary: Practise by reaching for a low shelf; people with back problems should ask a professional about what is right for them.

beats.scene: Grace leans against a wall with her hands flat and bends her arms slowly
beats.summary: Move four is the push: pushing a door, getting up from the floor, or pressing something away.

beats.scene: Grace does a wall press-up in her living room, standing at an angle
beats.summary: Wall press-ups are a gentle way to start, and a worktop or a low table can make it harder.

beats.scene: Mateo checks Grace's shoulders as she presses a light weight overhead
beats.summary: Pushing a light weight overhead, or moving things onto a high shelf, trains the shoulders too, but should be done carefully.

beats.scene: Grace counts pushes in her notebook with a smile at a kitchen counter
beats.summary: Practise two or three times a week, and add a few repetitions or a harder version as you improve.

beats.scene: Grace pulls open a heavy shop door with both hands in the rain
beats.summary: Move five is the pull: opening doors, pulling a bag towards you, or drawing a rope or a band.

beats.scene: A woman sits at a desk with rounded shoulders, then straightens up
beats.summary: Good posture is helped by a strong upper back, so pulling movements balance the effects of sitting.

beats.scene: Grace pulls a rubber band toward her chest with her elbows back
beats.summary: A rubber band tied to a door handle makes a simple home row.

beats.scene: Grace pulls a bucket up from a garden well with careful hands
beats.summary: Pull in daily life too: pulling up weeds, hauling a bag or carrying the washing; always keep a steady, controlled motion.

beats.scene: Grace carries two shopping bags along the pavement, one in each hand
beats.summary: Move six is the carry: lifting something and walking with it, such as shopping bags, a suitcase or a child.

beats.scene: Grace carries a watering can in each hand, standing tall
beats.summary: Carrying with a weight in each hand keeps the body balanced, and trains grip, shoulders and the stomach muscles.

beats.scene: A hand squeezes a rubber ball next to a drawing of a handshake
beats.summary: Grip strength is linked to general health in studies, though that does not mean grip alone causes it.

beats.scene: Grace walks across her garden with two filled watering cans, upright and smiling
beats.summary: Start with a light load and a short distance, and add weight and distance a little at a time.

beats.scene: Grace stands at the bottom of a staircase in her house, looking up
beats.summary: Move seven is climbing: stairs, steps and slopes, which work the legs, heart and lungs.

beats.scene: Grace goes up a staircase slowly, holding the handrail with one hand
beats.summary: Go up stairs steadily with a hand near a rail, step on the whole foot, and take the stairs one at a time.

beats.scene: Grace steps up onto the bottom stair and down again with a smile
beats.summary: Practise by stepping up onto the bottom stair repeatedly, then use more steps when it feels easy.

beats.scene: Grace walks up a gentle hill in the park on a sunny day
beats.summary: Short bursts of stair climbing are linked with better fitness, and any slope counts.

beats.scene: Grace turns her upper body to look over her shoulder while sitting
beats.summary: Move eight is the twist: turning to look behind you, reaching for a seat belt, or swinging a golf club.

beats.scene: Grace turns her upper body in a chair, arms crossed over her chest
beats.summary: Practise a gentle seated twist, turning slowly side to side, and never forcing it.

beats.scene: Grace reaches for a cup on a high shelf, turning her body gently
beats.summary: Add twisting to other moves slowly, such as reaching or turning with a light weight, and stop if it hurts.

beats.scene: A relaxed Grace unrolls a mat in front of a window in morning sun
beats.summary: A little stretching after exercise, while the body is warm, can help you feel looser, though it is not essential.

beats.scene: Grace stands on one leg while holding a kitchen counter
beats.summary: Move nine is balance: keeping steady while standing, walking or moving, which tends to decline with age unless practised.

beats.scene: A street with older people walking carefully, and a sign about falls
beats.summary: About one in three adults over sixty-five falls each year, and balance and strength training can reduce the risk.

beats.scene: Grace stands on one foot near a counter with her hand lightly touching it
beats.summary: Practise standing on one leg near a counter, holding on lightly, then try without your hands.

beats.scene: Grace walks a heel to toe line on the floor with arms slightly outstretched
beats.summary: Other balance practice includes walking heel to toe, and tai chi has good evidence for reducing falls.

beats.scene: Grace sits on a carpet in her living room beside a firm sofa
beats.summary: Move ten is getting down to the floor and up again, a skill that many of us lose without noticing.

beats.scene: Grace kneels with one knee down and a hand on a sturdy sofa
beats.summary: Practise next to a sturdy sofa or chair, going down onto one knee and then the floor, using your hands for support.

beats.scene: Grace places a cushion under her knee and a hand on a chair seat
beats.summary: Use a cushion, a chair and your own pace; never rush or force the movement, and ask for help if needed.

beats.scene: Grace and a small child play with building blocks together on the floor
beats.summary: With practice, getting down and up becomes easy, and it lets her play on the floor with her grandchild.

beats.scene: Grace pins a weekly plan with all ten moves on her fridge
beats.summary: Put the ten moves together in a simple week: walking most days, strength moves on two or three days, balance daily.

beats.scene: Grace sits on a park bench with her eyes closed and a calm look
beats.summary: Rest days matter, so listen to your body: tiredness is normal, but sharp pain, chest pain or dizziness are reasons to stop.

beats.scene: Grace sits in a doctor's waiting room with a notebook on her lap
beats.summary: People with health conditions should check with their doctor before starting, and a professional can adapt the moves.

beats.scene: Grace walks in a park with two friends who laugh together
beats.summary: Moving with others makes it more fun and easier to keep up, so invite a friend, join a class or walk with a neighbour.

beats.scene: Grace stands tall at the same kerb a year later, smiling in the sun
beats.summary: A year later Grace walks the same street with ease, stronger and more confident, and she enjoys moving again.

beats.scene: Grace and Mateo wave across the garden fence on a sunny morning
beats.summary: Walk, stand, bend, push, pull, carry, climb, twist, balance and get up from the floor: practise a little each day; this book is general information and not medical advice.

B1B2: Grace is sixty-three, and one morning she catches her foot on a kerb. She does not fall, but the shock stays with her, and she decides to look after her body.
Grace tells her neighbour Mateo, a physiotherapist, about her stumble. He smiles and says that the body is made to move, and that ten simple moves cover most of daily life.
Many of us sit for most of the day, at desks, in cars and in front of screens. Studies link long periods of sitting with poorer health, so it helps to get up often.
Health guidelines for adults suggest about 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity each week. That sounds like a lot, but some movement is always better than none, and you can start small.
The first move is walking, which is the base of almost everything else. It costs nothing, needs no equipment and can be done almost anywhere.
A brisk walk is one in which you breathe a little harder but can still hold a conversation. Mateo calls this the talk test, and it is a simple way to judge moderate effort.
Regular walking is linked with a healthier heart, stronger bones and a better mood. Large studies also suggest that people who walk more tend to live longer.
Grace begins with a ten-minute walk after breakfast every morning. Each week she adds a few minutes, until a half-hour walk feels like a normal part of her day.
The second move is standing up from a chair, which is really a squat in disguise. We do it many times each day, so we need legs that are strong enough.

To practise, Grace puts her feet flat and a little apart, leans her body forward and stands up by pushing through her feet. Then she sits down slowly, and she keeps full control of the movement all the way.
Some health professionals use a simple test: how many times can you stand up from a chair in thirty seconds? It is only a rough guide, but it shows whether your legs are getting stronger.
Grace practises standing up from her chair a few times each day, perhaps while the kettle boils. When it feels easy, she lowers herself more slowly or holds a bag of books against her chest.
The third move is the hinge, which is a way of bending at the hips and not at the back. We use it whenever we pick something up from the floor or a low shelf.
To hinge, Grace pushes her hips back as if she were closing a door with them. She keeps her back long and lets her knees bend a little as she reaches toward the floor.
When she lifts something heavy, Grace holds it close to her body and stands up using her legs and hips. A load held far from the body is much harder on the back.
Grace practises the hinge by reaching for things on a low shelf and tidying the floor. Anyone with back problems should ask a doctor or physiotherapist what is right for them.
The fourth move is the push, which we use to open heavy doors, push a trolley or press ourselves up from the floor. It works the chest, the shoulders and the back of the arms.
Grace starts with wall press-ups, standing a step from the wall and bending her elbows slowly. Later she moves to a kitchen counter, and then perhaps to a low table.
Pressing a light weight above the head can also train the shoulders. Grace uses a small tin of soup at first, and she stops if she feels any sharp pain.
Grace practises her pushing two or three times a week, and she writes down how many she can do. When it feels easy, she adds a few more or tries a harder version.
The fifth move is the pull, which we use to open doors, drag a bin or draw a bag towards us. It works the muscles of the upper back and the arms.
Many of us spend the day leaning forward over a desk or a phone. A strong upper back helps us to sit and stand more upright, and pulling movements build that strength.

Grace ties a rubber band to a sturdy door handle and pulls it toward her chest, squeezing her shoulder blades together. She does about ten slow pulls and then rests for a minute before she begins again.
Grace also notices pulling in everyday tasks, such as pulling up weeds or dragging a bag of leaves across the lawn. She keeps her movements steady, and she does not jerk.
The sixth move is the carry, which simply means picking something up and walking with it. We carry shopping, suitcases, laundry, grandchildren and even our own bags.
When Grace carries two bags, one in each hand, her body stays balanced. This trains her grip, her shoulders and her stomach muscles all at once.
Studies have found that grip strength is linked to general health and a longer life. This does not mean that a strong grip causes good health, but it is a useful sign.
Grace starts with two light bags and a short distance across the garden. Each week she adds a little more weight or walks a little farther.
The seventh move is climbing, which means going up stairs, steps or slopes. It makes the legs work harder and raises the heart rate, so it is good for fitness.
Grace goes up the stairs steadily, with one hand near the rail and her whole foot on each step. There is no hurry, and safety matters more than speed.
To practise, Grace steps up onto the bottom stair and down again, using the rail for balance. When it feels easy, she moves on to two or three steps.
Studies suggest that short bursts of stair climbing can improve fitness, even if you only do them a few times a day. Any slope counts, so a hill on the way to the shops is a bonus.
The eighth move is the twist, which is turning the upper body while the hips stay still. We twist to look behind us, to reach a seat belt or to dry our backs.
Grace sits tall in a chair, crosses her arms over her chest and turns her upper body slowly to each side. She moves only as far as feels comfortable and never forces it.
As she gets better, Grace adds some twisting to other movements, such as turning while holding a light weight. She keeps every movement slow and stops if anything hurts.
After exercise, when her muscles are warm, Grace does a few gentle stretches. Researchers say that stretching is not essential, but she enjoys it and it makes her feel looser.
The ninth move is balance, which means staying steady while you stand, walk or turn. Balance tends to get worse with age unless we practise it.
About one in three adults over sixty-five has a fall each year. Exercise programmes that include balance and leg strength have been shown to reduce the risk.
To practise, Grace stands on one leg near the kitchen counter, with a hand ready to touch it. When she feels steady, she holds on less and tries it with her eyes open for longer.
Grace also tries walking heel to toe along a straight line in the hallway. Mateo tells her that tai chi, a slow Chinese exercise, has good evidence for reducing falls in older adults.
The tenth move is getting down to the floor and up again, which is a skill that many people lose without noticing. It matters for playing with children, for gardening and for getting up after a fall.
Grace practises next to a sturdy sofa, going down onto one knee and then to the floor, with her hands for support. She does it slowly, and she has someone nearby the first time.
A cushion under the knee and a chair to push on can make the movement easier. Grace never rushes, and she asks for help if she needs it.
After some weeks of practice, Grace can get down to the floor and up again quite easily. She can now play with her young neighbour's daughter, who is delighted to have her company.
Grace makes a simple weekly plan: walking most days, strength moves on two or three days and a few minutes of balance each day. It takes about as long as watching one television programme.
Rest days are an important part of the plan, so Grace listens to her body. Tiredness is normal, but sharp pain, chest pain or dizziness are reasons to stop and speak to a doctor.

Grace had checked with her doctor before starting, as Mateo had advised. Anyone with a health condition, an injury or a worry should do the same, because a professional can adapt the moves to suit the person.
Grace finds that moving is more fun with other people. She invites two friends to walk with her, and later she joins a friendly balance class at the local hall.
A year later, Grace walks along the same street and steps over the kerb without a thought. She is stronger and steadier, and she enjoys moving more than she has done in years.

Walk, stand, bend, push, pull, carry, climb, twist, balance and get up from the floor, and practise a little every day. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so please ask a doctor about your own health.
C1C2: Grace had been a teacher for thirty-five years and retired with a head full of plans, but one grey morning her foot caught the edge of a kerb and the pavement rushed towards her. A passing stranger steadied her arm before she fell, and she was entirely unhurt, yet she walked home slowly, shaken by how fast it had happened. By the time she reached her door she had made up her mind to take care of her body while she still could.

Over the garden fence, Grace told her neighbour Mateo about the stumble, and he listened with the calm attention of a man who had heard many such stories. Mateo was a physiotherapist, and he said cheerfully that the human body was built to move, and that most of what we do in a day is made up of about ten basic movements. If she practised those ten, he promised, she would be preparing for nearly everything that real life asks of her.

Mateo began by pointing out how much of modern life takes place in a chair, in the car, at a desk, in front of the television, and how rarely the average person is asked to move. Large studies link long hours of unbroken sitting with a higher risk of several health problems, although they cannot prove that sitting alone is the cause. The simple advice is to interrupt it often, and even a minute or two of standing and walking helps.

The World Health Organization advises adults to aim for about 150 to 300 minutes of moderate physical activity each week, together with some muscle-strengthening on two days or more. Mateo stressed that these figures are targets and not tests, and that any amount of movement is better than none, so there is no need to feel discouraged by a low starting point. Every extra step, he said, is a small deposit in a bank that pays interest for life.

The first of the ten moves, Mateo said, is the one that Grace already knew best, which is walking, and it is the foundation on which the other nine are built. It costs nothing, needs no equipment and can be fitted into the day almost anywhere, on the way to the shops, around the garden or up and down a long corridor. Its very ordinariness, he added, is exactly what makes people underestimate it, and what makes it so easy to begin.

How fast should Grace walk, she wondered, and how would she ever know whether she was going fast enough to matter? Mateo suggested the talk test, in which a brisk pace is one that leaves you breathing harder and warmer but still able to hold a conversation, though not to sing an aria. This level of effort counts as moderate activity, and it is the level that most of the health guidelines have in mind, although what feels brisk differs from one person to the next.

The benefits of walking are among the best studied in all of health research, and they include a healthier heart, better control of blood sugar, stronger bones and improved mood. Large studies also suggest that people who walk more tend to live longer, though people who walk more are often healthier in other ways too, so the exact size of the effect is hard to measure. It is, in any case, one of the cheapest and most pleasant ways of looking after yourself that anyone has ever found.

Mateo advised her not to begin with a heroic hike but with something that she could not possibly fail, which was a ten-minute stroll every morning after breakfast. After a week she added two minutes, then two more, and by the end of the month she was walking for half an hour without any thought of stopping. Habits that begin small, he reminded her, are the ones that tend to last.

The second move was one that Grace performed a dozen times a day without a second thought, namely standing up from a chair. Mateo called it a squat in disguise, and he pointed out that the same leg strength lets a person get out of the car or up from the sofa without help. It is, in a very practical sense, the move that keeps us independent for as long as possible.

Mateo showed her how to do it properly: place the feet flat on the floor and slightly apart, lean the chest forward over the toes, and drive upward by pushing through the feet until the body is upright. The lowering, he said, is as important as the rising, so she should sit down slowly and with control rather than dropping into the seat. If a chair felt too low, she could raise it with a firm cushion until she grew stronger.

Physiotherapists sometimes use a simple test to get a rough picture of leg strength, which is to count how many times a person can stand up from a chair in thirty seconds. Grace tried it with Mateo holding the stopwatch, and she managed a modest number that she did not particularly want to share. The figure, he said, matters less than the direction in which it moves, and he asked her to try it again in a month.

Mateo asked her to practise a few stands from her chair each day, ideally while waiting for the kettle to boil, so that no extra time was needed. Once the movement felt easy, she could make it harder in several ways: by lowering herself more slowly, by using a lower seat or by holding a bag of books against her chest. Progress, in his view, is simply a matter of asking the muscles for a little more than they are used to.

Bending is something that every person does every day, but the third move, the hinge, is a particular way of doing it, in which the movement comes from the hips and not from the curve of the back. We use it whenever we pick up a laundry basket, empty a dishwasher or lift a toddler, and a good hinge spreads the work over the powerful muscles of the buttocks and legs. It is gentler on the spine than a rounded stoop, Mateo said, and it is easy to learn with a little practice.

Mateo asked Grace to stand with her hands on her thighs and push her hips backwards, as though she were trying to close a drawer behind her with them. Her knees bent slightly, her back stayed long and her chest tipped forward, and she could feel the muscles at the back of her legs begin to work. Nothing about it was complicated, he said, but it was a pattern that most people had stopped using.

In the garden, Grace put the hinge to work on a bag of compost, bending her knees, keeping the load close to her body and standing up by driving through her legs and hips. Mateo explained that a weight held far from the body places more strain on the back, so the nearer it travels to the centre, the easier it is to lift safely. There is no single perfect way to lift, he added, but this is a sensible habit that works for most people.

Grace practised the hinge whenever she reached for a saucepan on the bottom shelf, put on her shoes or picked up a fallen newspaper, until it began to feel natural. Mateo reminded her that every body is different, and that anyone with back pain, a disc problem or an old injury should ask a doctor or a physiotherapist what is right for their own body. General advice, he said, can never replace a proper assessment by someone who has examined you in person.

The fourth move is the push, and Grace realised that she had been using it for decades without a name, to open heavy doors, to shove a loaded trolley and to raise herself from a chair arm. It works the chest, the shoulders and the backs of the arms, and it is among the first movements to be neglected by people who spend their days sitting down. Fortunately, it is also one of the easiest to practise at home, with nothing more than a wall and a little time.

Mateo's recommended starting point was the wall press-up, in which one stands a short step away from a wall, places the hands at shoulder height and bends the elbows until the face approaches the wall. As she grew stronger, Grace moved to the kitchen counter, where the greater slope made the work harder, and eventually she might try a low table or even the floor. The art is to find a version that is difficult but manageable, and to move up only when it begins to feel easy.

Pushing upward is a little different from pushing forward, and it is just as useful for putting a suitcase on a high shelf or a plate in an upper cupboard. Mateo had Grace practise with a pair of tins of soup, pressing them overhead with a firm stomach and relaxed neck and stopping the moment she felt any sharp pain in the shoulders. The old maxim of starting light applies here more strongly than almost anywhere else in the body.

Two or three short sessions each week were enough, Mateo said, and Grace jotted down how many repetitions she managed in a small notebook on the kitchen windowsill. When the number began to feel easy, she added another few repetitions or chose a slightly harder version, and within a month she was pleased to see the figures rising. Gentle, regular effort, he told her, tends to beat occasional heroics, and it is far kinder to the joints.

The fifth move is the pull, which brings things, and sometimes the body, towards the centre, and Grace noticed it in the effort of opening a heavy shop door in the rain. It works the muscles of the upper back and the backs of the shoulders, as well as the arms, and it balances the pushing movements that dominate so much of the day. Without it, Mateo observed, the shoulders tend to drift forward into a permanent slouch.

Most of us spend a great deal of the day with our shoulders rolled forward, whether over a desk, a steering wheel or a telephone, and the muscles of the upper back are rarely asked to work. Mateo explained that strengthening them can help a person to sit and stand more upright, although posture is complicated and no single position is correct for everyone. Variety, and regular movement, matter far more than a rigid attempt to hold a perfect pose.

Grace's home equipment consisted of a long rubber band, which Mateo tied securely to a door handle, and a chair on which she sat facing the door. She drew the band towards her chest with her elbows tucked back, gently squeezing her shoulder blades together, and then let it return slowly, repeating the movement about ten times. Cheap, light and endlessly adjustable, a rubber band is a remarkable piece of gym equipment.

Once she had learned to recognise the pull, Grace saw it everywhere: in tugging weeds out of the flower bed, in dragging a sack of leaves across the lawn and in hauling the washing basket up from the cellar. She learned to keep these movements smooth, to keep her back long and to avoid sudden jerks, which strain the muscles more than steady effort. Training, she was discovering, was simply daily life carried out with a little more care and a little more attention.

The sixth move, the carry, was the simplest of all to describe: pick something up and take it somewhere else. We do it with shopping bags, suitcases, laundry baskets, watering cans and sometimes with grandchildren, and a person who can do it comfortably is very likely to remain independent for a long time. Everyday life, Mateo said, is very largely a series of carries separated by moments of rest.

Mateo suggested that she carry a weight in each hand rather than a single heavy load on one side, because an equal burden keeps the body balanced and the posture upright. In doing so she was training her grip, her shoulders and her stomach muscles all together, with no need for an expensive machine or a membership card. She also found that the walk home from the shops had somehow become a workout.

Researchers have noticed that the strength of a person's grip is associated with general health and even with longevity in older adults, which is why doctors sometimes measure it. This does not prove that squeezing a ball will make you live longer, since a strong grip may simply be a sign of a body that is strong and active in other ways. It is nevertheless a useful reminder that our hands deserve some attention too, since we use them in almost everything we do.

Mateo told her to begin with a load that felt only moderately demanding, perhaps two half-filled watering cans, and to carry them across the garden and back at a steady pace. Every week she added a little more weight or a little more distance, never both at once, and she stopped at once if she felt pain, dizziness or breathlessness. A small, patient increase is the secret of almost every kind of progress, and the carry is no exception to that rule.

The seventh move was climbing, whether on a staircase, on the steps of a bus or on the gentle slope of a hill, and it was the one that Grace had been most inclined to avoid. It asks the legs, the heart and the lungs to work together against gravity, and it is therefore one of the most efficient forms of everyday exercise. Hills and stairs, Mateo said, are free gyms that most of us walk past every day.

Safety came first, Mateo emphasised, so Grace practised going up her staircase at a steady pace, with one hand near the rail, her whole foot on each step and her eyes ahead. Speed was beside the point, because the goal was strength and confidence and not a record, and she could always rest on a landing if she needed to. Anyone who feels dizzy, unsteady or chest-tight on stairs should speak to a doctor.

For a gentler beginning, Mateo suggested that Grace simply step up onto the bottom stair and back down again, holding the rail and leading with alternate legs, ten times in a row. Once that became easy, she graduated to two or three steps and later to a full flight, each stage building on the last in a pleasantly logical order. Soon the staircase, which she had regarded with some suspicion, had become an old friend.

Research suggests that even short bursts of stair climbing, repeated several times a day, can measurably improve fitness in people who are otherwise inactive. Any slope counts as well, so a hill on the way to the shops is a bonus rather than a burden, and Grace began to choose the longer route on purpose. A long-term habit built from many tiny efforts, Mateo reminded her, is the most reliable kind.

The eighth move, the twist, was one that Grace had never thought of as exercise at all, although she used it whenever she reversed the car, reached for a seat belt or turned to speak to a passenger. It means rotating the upper body while the hips stay largely still, and it is surprisingly important for flexibility of the spine and for many sports. A body that has forgotten how to turn is a body that has begun to stiffen, Mateo said.

A gentle seated twist was Mateo's recommendation, and Grace performed it sitting upright on the edge of a sturdy chair, arms crossed over her chest, turning slowly to the right and then to the left. She went only as far as felt comfortable, breathed steadily and avoided any jerk, since twisting suddenly under strain is a classic way of injuring the back. Control is always more important than range in this move, and gentleness is always better than force.

As the seated twist became comfortable, Grace began to combine turning with other movements, reaching across her body for a cup or rotating gently while holding a light tin of beans. Mateo insisted that all of this be done slowly and in complete control, and that she stop if anything hurt, especially in the back or the hips. People who have back problems should ask a physiotherapist before they start any twisting exercises.

After her sessions, while her muscles were still warm, Grace enjoyed a few minutes of gentle stretching, holding each position for about half a minute without bouncing. Researchers still debate how much stretching matters for avoiding injury or improving performance, and it is certainly not essential, but many people find that it feels pleasant and leaves them looser. If it feels good and does not hurt, Mateo said, there is no reason to leave it out.

The ninth move was balance, the quiet skill that lies behind every step, and one that most people never practise until it has begun to fail. Because balance depends on the eyes, the inner ear, the muscles and the nerves working together, it can decline with age, but the encouraging news is that it responds well to practice. This, Mateo said, was the move that had been waiting for Grace on that grey morning at the kerb.

Mateo told her that about one in three adults over the age of sixty-five falls at least once a year, which was a sobering figure but not a hopeless one. Reviews of many studies have found that exercise programmes that include balance training and leg strengthening can reduce the number of falls, and the effect is greater when the exercises are challenging and regular. Falling, in other words, is not an inevitable part of growing older, and there is a great deal that a person can do.

Beside the kitchen counter, with a hand hovering just above it for safety, Grace lifted one foot a few centimetres from the floor and tried to stay perfectly still. The first few attempts were wobbly and a little comic, but within a week she could hold the position for twenty seconds, and she began to touch the counter less and less. The key rule, Mateo said, is to practise somewhere that you can grab something firm, and never on a slippery floor.

Heel-to-toe walking along a line in the hallway became part of Grace's routine, and so did turning her head slowly while she walked, which made the exercise more challenging. Mateo mentioned that tai chi, the slow and graceful exercise that began in China, has been shown in several studies to reduce falls in older adults, and she added a local class to her list of things to try. Balance, he said, is the move to practise a little every day, even if only for the length of a song.

The tenth move was perhaps the most surprising of all, since it is simply the ability to get down on to the floor and up again, a skill that children perform without thinking and many adults quietly lose. It matters for playing with grandchildren, for gardening, for finding something under the bed and, above all, for getting up after a fall. Grace admitted that she had not sat on her own living room floor for about ten years.

With a firm sofa beside her and Mateo standing close, Grace lowered herself carefully onto one knee, then the other, and finally sat on the carpet, using her hands for support whenever she needed them. Getting up was harder, and it took three attempts to find the sequence of hands, knee and foot that suited her body, but when she stood she gave a small, triumphant laugh. Someone should always be nearby for the first few attempts, Mateo advised, in case a little help is needed.

A cushion beneath the knee, a sturdy chair to push against and a comfortable pace were the three things that made the movement manageable, and Grace used all of them. She was told never to rush, never to force a painful position and never to feel embarrassed about asking for help, since nobody has ever grown stronger by pretending to be stronger than they are. Patience is part of the technique here too, and so is a good sense of humour.

After several weeks of daily practice, Grace found that she could lower herself to the carpet and stand up again with a fluency that would have astonished her in the spring. When her young neighbour's daughter came to visit, she knelt beside the child and built towers of coloured blocks for an hour, and was surprised to find that she was not tired but happy. It had been a long time since she had been at eye level with a child.

With all ten moves learned, Grace pinned a simple plan to the fridge: a walk on most days, the strength moves two or three times a week, and a few minutes of balance and floor practice daily. The whole thing took little longer than watching an episode of her favourite programme, and it fitted comfortably into a normal life. A modest plan that you follow is better than a magnificent one that you do not.

Mateo was firm that rest is part of training, and he asked Grace to listen to her body with the same attention that she had once given to her pupils. Muscle tiredness and mild stiffness are a normal reward for effort, he said, but sharp pain, chest pain, unusual breathlessness, dizziness or sudden weakness are signs to stop at once and to speak to a doctor. No exercise plan is worth ignoring a warning from your own body, however keen you are to carry on.

At Mateo's suggestion, Grace had mentioned her plan to her doctor at her annual check-up, and the doctor had approved with a nod and a smile. Anyone with a heart condition, high blood pressure, osteoporosis, a joint problem, an injury or simply a worry about starting should do the same, since a doctor or physiotherapist can adapt the moves to suit the individual. The ten moves are a general framework and not a personal prescription, and a professional can help to adjust them.

Grace discovered that the best way to keep going was to keep company, and she invited two old friends from the school staff room to walk with her every Thursday morning. They talked far more than they walked, at first, but the miles accumulated nonetheless, and before long they had joined a friendly balance class at the local hall. Movement shared, she decided, was a pleasure doubled, and it was far harder to skip when someone was waiting.

A year after her stumble, Grace walked down the same street on a bright autumn morning and stepped off the kerb without a second thought, her stride long and her balance sure. She was stronger and steadier than she had been for a decade, and she moved through the world with a lightness that surprised even her. The ten moves had not turned her into an athlete, but they had given her back her confidence.

Walk, stand, bend, push, pull, carry, climb, twist, balance and rise from the floor: these ten moves are the ordinary movements of a lifetime, and a little practice each day helps to keep them yours. Start gently, listen to your body and be patient, because strength and balance can improve at any age. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so please speak to a doctor or a physiotherapist about your own health and your own needs.
